inline.s: The next morning we skipped our morning gruel, bore our hunger, and went straight into the abbot's quarters to bow. The Master asked, 'Where do you two come from?' We answered, 'From Yunnan.' He asked again, 'What have you come here to do?' Because we had no robe or bowl, we did not dare say we had come to seek the precepts, and said only that we had come to pay homage at Mount Wutai. The Master said, 'Manjushri is right there where you are, and yet you come to pay homage to the terrace! Go back and practice mindful recitation yourselves!' Because of this the two of us made a vow: if in future we should become good teachers, we would never accept the ceremonial courtesies of monks from elsewhere, so that those poor Chan meditators might find it easier to meet us.

So we went up the mountain and came to Tayuan Temple. Two of the monks living in the quarters here were fellow disciples who had made the vow to recite the Five Great Sutras over three years. They questioned us, learned that we had come a long way from Yunnan, and were delighted to have us stay. Chengzhuo volunteered to carry water for the monks and let me enter the hall to recite sutras. When he had finished carrying water, he devoted himself to reading the Lotus Sutra. Apart from attending the shrine for services, I spent my spare time reading the Shurangama Meaning Ocean. The two of us spoke no idle words and let our legs wander nowhere; each day we rested only at midnight. On Mount Wutai, all the temples great and small took porridge made from oat flour as their food. The abbot of Tayuan Temple, whose dharma name was Deyun, and the monks of the quarters, seeing how diligently the two of us studied and that after more than a month there was not the slightest change in us, all conceived a mind of faith and respect toward us and privately invited us to eat rice gruel. Chengzhuo and I discussed it and said, 'Studying late into the night among all these monks disturbs their sleep. In the Sangharama Hall (the hall enshrining the temple's protective deities) over there a glass lamp is lit at night, and no one is inside. We would do better to go there and study by the light of the glass lamp; thus we would not hinder others, and our minds would be still and concentrated, which is good for memory. We will stop when the night grows quiet.' On Mount Wutai, spring and autumn are already very cold; how much more so in winter! By the tenth month our clothing was thin. Holding the sutra scrolls and standing upright in the lamplight, our attention wholly gathered, we felt nothing at all. But when we closed the scrolls to rest, our fingers were so stiff we could not bend or stretch them, our legs so numb with cold we could hardly step, and our whole bodies shivered, the cold piercing to our very lungs. Even so, our resolve grew only firmer.

The spring that followed was the ninth year of Chongzhen. At the end of the second month, Juexin came back to Nanjing from his pilgrimage to the sea and searched for us the whole way, arriving at Mount Wutai to meet us. In the middle of the third month a monk came to pay homage at Mount Wutai, a man of Chu (the region of Hubei), whose dharma name was Jiaoru. We had once been together at Baoqing Prefecture, hearing Master Zhuanyu expound the Shurangama Four Reliances, and seeing us in the hall he came in to greet us. When someone asked how he had come to know us, he told the whole story of our pilgrimage in detail. When the abbot Master Deyun learned of it, he prepared a vegetarian feast and gathered the whole community, asking me to lecture on the Shurangama Sutra beginning the first day of the fourth month. I received this kindness, but could not find a way to decline, and so had to accept. It was not until the first day of the seventh month that the lectures were completed. The three of us had first come to Mount Wutai and had lived all along at Tayuan Temple, and had never paid homage at the Buddha shrines of the five peaks, so on the third day of the seventh month we went first to the East Terrace. The abbot there entertained us with the courtesy due a Dharma Master. Then we went on to the North Terrace, and the resident monk there received us in the same way. I felt shame in my heart at this, and did not go to pay homage at the other terraces.

On the eighth day we took leave of the abbot of Tayuan Temple and the monks of every quarter, intending to go to Beijing to seek the precepts from Master Sanmei. The abbot earnestly urged us to stay, and when he saw that we had no heart to remain, he prepared three mules to see me, Chengzhuo, and Juexin off, and accompanied us all the way to Jiulu Ridge, where we stayed the night. The next morning Master Deyun still could not bear to part, and escorted us on to the lower courtyard at the Tangli Tree. When day broke he invited us to a vegetarian meal, and only then did we take our leave of him one by one. As we parted, Master Deyun, tears in his eyes, repeatedly urged us, saying, 'When you have received the precepts, please come back to Mount Wutai. Do not disappoint our earnest hopes.'
On the nineteenth day of the seventh month we came west of Fangshun Bridge in Baoding Prefecture and lodged at the Luo
Muhou

Temple. While at Mount Wutai, Chengzhuo had made an appointment with a Daoist from Cangzhou, so he went to Cangzhou. The next afternoon Juexin and I went out of the temple gate to stroll, and far off we saw a grove of trees, deep and green with shade. The six of us who had come out together walked into the grove, and because we craved the coolness we sat a while too long, until the sun was nearly sinking in the west. Just then, as we thought of rising to return to the temple, we saw the sky filled with a grey haze like mist, and heard a chattering, twittering din. Gradually we made out flying dust rolling and surging like clouds. Before long we saw countless men and women, old and young, spread across the fields, all racing wildly, rushing toward us like a landslide or a surging sea. Only then did we understand that soldiers and horses were pursuing them from behind. The people who had been sitting together in the grove scattered in every direction, and only Juexin stayed with me. We could not go back to the temple any longer, nor could we take the highway, so we fled in confusion toward the south. The places we lodged along the way were mostly small temples, and each day we could eat only one meal.

We crossed every ditch and forded every stream, took wrong turns and went roundabout ways, and so pressed on. One day on the road my belly felt desperately hungry, so we rested under a tree beside a stagnant pool, and I said to Juexin, 'We have gone from Yunnan to the south, and from the south to Beijing. Now again we go from north to south, more than twenty thousand li back and forth, toiling in vain, and the vow we made has not been fulfilled. The purpose for which my ordaining master gave me the dharma name Shaoru was the hope that I might spread the Dharma and benefit beings. As things now stand, all of that is utterly cut off, and my shame is beyond words! My dharma name is Dubi: bi means the body, that is, the essential body of the Dharma; only by reading the sutras and teachings can one understand the principle they set forth; once the principle is understood, the words that explain it may be forgotten. It is like using a finger to point out the moon: once you have seen the moon, you need no longer attend to the finger; the principle is the same. Now I want to change my name to see the moon.' The two of us turned it over and over, thinking and thinking, and the more we thought the more sorrowful we felt, until tears of grief fell of themselves in streams. Just then an old man passed by, and seeing how bitterly the two of us grieved, he came over to ask the reason. I told him in detail of the pain of our long pilgrimage and our failure to fulfil our vow. The old man sighed again and again, and said to us, 'My surname is Li. I am a Daoist who keeps a long fast, alone with no kin. I teach children for other families, and because of the chaos of soldiers and horses I have come home; my house is in the small village just ahead. I beg you to come and stay the night with me before going on.' When we reached his house we saw that robbers had stripped it bare, so he went to a neighbour to borrow some coarse flour and baked cakes for us to eat. The next day we took our leave of him and set out.

We walked six days more and came out on the highway at Nangong County. By afternoon we had found no place to beg a meal, and far off we saw a small hermitage. When we reached the gate of the hermitage, Juexin stayed outside and I went in alone. I saw an old monk with no one to help him, kindling the fire and cooking for himself. I joined my palms and greeted him, and he did not return the greeting. So I went up and kindled the fire for him. When the food was cooked he served himself rice and sat down to eat. I too took a bowl and chopsticks myself, filled my bowl, sat down, and began to eat, and I said nothing either. When he had eaten one bowl, I filled a second. Only then did he speak: 'I have never in this world seen anyone like you. The host had not spoken, yet you helped yourself and began eating.' I answered, 'I have never in this world seen anyone like you. A guest stands before you, and you do not even offer a polite word inviting him to eat, so I helped myself.' He looked at me and laughed aloud, saying, 'So you are a Chan meditator after all. When I was young I went out to call on good teachers and wandered everywhere on pilgrimage, and because I was not seasoned I often went hungry. Today you are in that same case; please eat as much as you like!' I said, 'There is a fellow practitioner outside the gate.' When he heard this he was very glad, and said, 'Invite him in to eat with us.' Juexin and I ate our fill, and when we rose to take our leave he would not allow it, and kept us three days more.

At the beginning of the ninth month we came to Guazhou in Jiangnan and registered our stay at Xilang Hermitage. There we met a monk from Yunnan whose name was Qingru. In talking of our pilgrimage we learned that he had met with the calamity of soldiers and horses in the north and had only then come back south. The next day he crossed the river with Juexin and me and went on to Ganlu Temple. The resident master's dharma name was Pingsu; he too was a fellow provincial, long resident in Zhenjiang Prefecture, and many people had taken refuge in him and believed in him. He was especially fond of people from Yunnan who came to Jiangnan to study. Qingru went in first to announce us, and Juexin and I followed and went in to bow. Master Pingsu asked us about the hardships we had met on pilgrimage, and I concealed nothing and told him the truth. Master Pingsu comforted us, saying, 'In my youth when I went out to call on teachers I too met with many adverse circumstances, yet my mind seeking the Way never fell back in the least, and only thus do I have this small karmic connection today. You two have sought a teacher and sought the precepts, going back and forth north and south, through every kind of hardship, and the vow you made at the outset has not slackened; in future the conditions for you to teach and guide living beings will surely be most excellent. For now, set your hearts at ease and stay here. At the New Year, the first day of the tenth year of Chongzhen, comes my mother's suffering day (the day his mother gave him birth), and I will recite the Five Great Sutras to repay my mother's kindness. The two of you may recite with the community. As for robes and bedding, I will see to them for you. When the recitation period is over, it will not be too late to go.' I said, 'Master Sanmei is far away in Beijing; we cannot go there again, so we must wait for him to return south before seeking the precepts. For now I want to go to Tiantong Temple to practice Chan.' Master Pingsu gave his support, and besides providing us with travelling gear he gave each of us two taels and five mace of silver for the road.

On the third day of the second month we arrived at the bridgehead of Danyang County, wanting to take a passenger boat across the river. Juexin set the luggage down at his feet and gave all his attention to watching the boatmen jostle one another and compete for passengers, and in that moment our bundle of luggage was stolen. We could only sigh at how our karmic conditions had come to such a pass! Fortunately my travel money was still on my person. Toward noon we came to Haihui Hermitage to lodge, and when they saw we had brought no luggage they would not give us a place. We told them the luggage had been lost at the bridgehead. The hermitage was not far from the bridgehead, and when they had gone and learned that it was indeed true, they sent us into the Cloud and Water Hall (where wandering monks are given temporary lodging). There we met two wandering monks who had travelled with us for several days when we were going north. Learning of our pilgrimage, they said, 'You are seeking the precepts, but Master Sanmei has already left Beijing; in the first month he opened the precept platform at Shita Temple in Yangzhou Prefecture. Now he has accepted the invitation of Haichao Hermitage in Dantu County, and the period begins on the eighth day of the second month. You had better hurry there to receive the precepts.' Hearing this news, the gloom pent up in my heart vanished like smoke and scattered clouds.

The next morning Juexin and I turned back to Haichao Hermitage, and it happened that we met Master Sanmei entering the hermitage. We heard that the Precept-Instructing Master (the monk responsible for teaching the newly ordained the ceremonies and the content of the precepts) was a man of Chu whose dharma name was Xunliu; he was broad of mind, subtle and skilful in wisdom, and most dignified in his guidance and teaching, and he directed all affairs throughout the precept period. So I asked the Guest-Receiving Master (the monk who receives visitors from outside) to lead me to the cell where Master Xunliu lived so that I might bow to him. The Master asked me my native place, and I answered, 'Yunnan.' He said, 'The resident master of this hermitage is opening the period to bury his own teacher; each person pays one tael of silver and provides his own robe and bowl.' I said, 'My luggage was lost completely at Danyang. All I have on me is two taels and three mace of travel money.' The Precept-Instructing Master said, 'That is only enough for one person to register and have a robe and bowl made.' I then begged a place for Juexin as well, and presently someone was sent to take me into the precept hall, while Juexin was sent to the quarters of the hall servers (those who do miscellaneous work).

The Master of Ceremonies of the new precept hall (the monk who looked after the daily life and discipline of newly arrived ordinands) had the dharma name Eryan. He was from Shandong, upright by nature but lacking in flexibility. Seeing that I had not the least luggage and did not request a Vinaya reader, that I sat all day on my own seat without speaking a word, that I broke none of the precept hall's rules and yet never came to consult him about anything, he grew very displeased with me and rebuked me, saying, 'Jianyue, this is no place for you to sit in silent Chan. Why do you not request the Vinaya Reader and study it thoroughly?' I answered, 'I cannot read, and I have no money to request the Vinaya Reader.' Whenever an ordinand came in and was given a seat, the Master of Ceremonies would call to me, 'Jianyue, come and sit here, and yield your seat to this newcomer.' I obeyed, picked up my robe and bowl, and moved back one seat. In this way more than ten people entered the hall after me, and with each one I was made to give up a seat. At last one more person entered the hall, and there was no seat left on the high platform (the long plank sleeping platform), so I was told to move down to the floor and sit together with the incense-and-lamp keeper (the monk in charge of incense and lamps in the hall). I murmured no complaint, but took it all as a game. The brother ordinands in the same hall, seeing this, were all indignant and said I was weak to the extreme. I said, 'Practice takes patience and forbearance as its root; and besides, we are all receiving the same precepts together, so it is only right that I should move and yield.'

As the time drew near for reciting the Vinaya for Daily Use from memory (before ordination one must first study the content of the precepts under the Precept-Instructing Master, learn them by heart in advance, and pass examination before one may mount the platform to receive the precepts), the Master of Ceremonies placed my name first on the list, intending to break and subdue me. The brother ordinands were anxious on my behalf too, saying, 'There is no way you can recite it; why not go and beg the Master of Ceremonies to put your name at the back?' I said, 'We shall see tomorrow.' Early the next day the Master of Ceremonies took the name slips and led nine of us before the Precept-Instructing Master. After we had bowed, I recited the whole text aloud in one breath, without the least hindrance, like water poured from a pitcher. The Precept-Instructing Master said, 'You sit in silence every day and speak no word; you said you could not read, and yet today you recite so fluently.' I said, 'It is not that I cannot read. Because I had no money to request the Vinaya books, I sat in silence and gave my whole mind to listening to the brother ordinands on my left and right recite, and so I remembered it.' The Precept-Instructing Master was very pleased and gave me tea to drink. When I returned to the hall, all my fellow ordinands came to congratulate me, and among them those most in tune with me, thirteen in all, were able to recite in the same way.

During this precept period the Brahma Net Sutra was studied. Master Acharya Xiangxue (the Precept Master) took the great seat (the principal seat) in place of the abbot, and the four heads of the assembly (the chief, western, rear, and hall seats) took turns lecturing again in review. One day the Chief Seat, whose dharma name was Leru, was giving a review lecture, and he merely read through the Direct Explanation written by Master Sanmei, adding not a word and taking away not a word, offering not the slightest explanation. Several of us ordinands who were in tune with one another sat in a row, exchanged glances and smiles, and let slip a laugh. The Chief Seat saw it and was very displeased. Returning to the hall, he named the ten of us to give review lectures. Never before had such a thing happened to newly ordained shramaneras; it was nothing but an improvised device to force us to go and confess to him. Three days passed and not one person came to seek pardon, so he could only submit the list he had drawn up to the abbot. Master Sanmei took it for a genuine recommendation and graciously approved them one and all. So the false was made true, and it could no longer be stopped.

On the day appointed for my review lecture, everyone inside and outside was astir, and all came to listen. The Master and the two venerable ones (Acharya Xiangxue and Precept-Instructing Master Xunliu) also set up seats behind and attended, graciously bestowing their blessing. The text to be expounded was the Ten Adamantine Seeds and the Tenth Stage of Faith from the upper fascicle of the Brahma Net Sutra. I opened the scroll, read the passage through, first summed up the general meaning, and then explained it according to the text. The audience below acclaimed me with one voice. Master Sanmei and the two venerable ones were all delighted. Then I went to the abbot's quarters to bow in thanks, and the Master bestowed on me bedding, robes, and shoes. Master Xunliu asked me, 'Under whom have you studied the sutras?' I said, 'In Yunnan I studied under my ordaining master. On pilgrimage at Baoqing Prefecture I met Master Ziru, who was lecturing on the Shurangama Four Reliances in place of Master Zhuanyu, and I also followed and listened.' Master Xunliu said, 'Master Zhuan is my own teacher in whom I take refuge, and Master Ziru is my close friend. Why did you not say so earlier!' He esteemed me all the more, and at once gave Juexin robes and bowl and had him enter the hall to receive the precepts.

On the twentieth day of the third month, after noon, a young scholar, the nephew of the He family of Danyang County, arrogant by nature and without faith in the Three Jewels, came drunk into the hermitage, pushed his way straight into the abbot's quarters, planted himself on the Master's dharma seat, and laughed and carried on without restraint. The attendant went up to remonstrate with him, and he only berated him in return. The monks of the temple were indignant and drove him out. Early the next morning this scholar gathered a crowd of men and came to the hermitage to stir up trouble. The Master at once ordered the precepts to be concluded and the period closed. Ordinarily the evening service in the temple was attended by many lay disciples who rejoiced in it. Master Xun wished to settle the affair by an expedient means and preserve the place of practice, so when the evening service was over he gathered everyone before the bodhisattva Weituo and said, 'Today this place of practice has been troubled and obstructed by demons, and cannot end as well as it began. Among you disciples, if there is anyone willing to give up body and life to protect the Dharma gate, let him come forward and bear it!' When he had spoken, all were silent. I answered the call, pushed through the crowd, and came forward, bowing to Master Xun. The Master said, 'You are only one man. How can you manage it?' I said, 'The Master's precept disciples are spread throughout the land. If I take the lead, the rest will follow. One who has left home has no wife to cling to, no property to bind him, no fame to preserve, no body or life to begrudge; he eats his fill from the alms bowl and carries not a cent; he dwells in the monastery groves and pays no rent. For every monk, the precepts are his kin; and all the more, to protect the Dharma gate, who would not bravely step forward! Even if it takes a year or two, the demon faction will surely be cleared away. I beg the Master and the two venerable ones to set their minds at ease and not to give it a thought. But if among that crowd there truly is a man willing to part with wife and property and to give up fame and life, let him stand out and try conclusions with me. Otherwise, let each household attend to its own studies and cultivate well the root of its own virtue. Since ancient times, when virtue and good writing were present, the scholars of the schools all attained rank and fame and were reckoned great men of the world. Would anyone be willing, over the rights and wrongs of another, to destroy all his own virtue?' Master Xun said, 'Today, in the presence of the assembly, you have made such a promise. Hereafter you must act according to your words. What fear is there that the Dharma gate will not be purified and the demonic obstacles not removed!' The assembly dispersed; all who had attended the evening service heard it, and the words were passed from one to another and spread far and wide.

At noon the next day more than twenty people did indeed come, all of them village elders and local household heads, and they came to the hermitage to pay their respects to Master Xunliu and also summoned me there, and the two sides settled the matter by reasoned discussion. The date for the completion of the precepts was not changed, and remained the eighth day of the fourth month. The Master gathered everyone in the abbot's quarters and said to the two venerable ones and to the senior monks who had long attended him, 'Had the demonic affair in this hall of practice not arisen today, Jianyue would never have shown himself. You who serve the Buddha-Dharma and act as teachers of others should have the same courage and the same resolve as he. In this precept-transmission period I have at last found a person of ability.' When the assembly heard this, they bowed in thanks and withdrew. The two venerable ones instructed and guided the thirteen of us who had been ordained together, that from then on we should attend the Master as his personal attendants, in the hope that we might become pillars of the Dharma.

On the tenth day we returned to Shita Temple in Yangzhou. Huizhao Temple in Yangzhou Prefecture invited the Master with due ceremony, and a date was chosen for opening the precept platform on the twentieth day of the fourth month. The eighth day of the fifth month was Master Sanmei's birthday, and none of us who had been ordained together had a gift to offer. I proposed, 'We could mount a long scroll and paint the Fifty-Three Visits on it ourselves and offer it to the Master in celebration of his birthday. That will leave me no time, so I cannot go with the rest of you to Huizhao Temple for the opening of the period.' When the Master heard of it he called me into the abbot's quarters to paint with a quiet mind, and said with a laugh, 'Jianyue, you have only just stepped onto the precept rank, and already you enter my room.' I bowed to the Master in shame and gave thanks. On the twentieth day of the sixth month the sea route commissioner, Master Zheng, invited the Master to hold a Ullambana assembly at Shita Temple and to lecture on the Xiaoheng Chao. The Master then ordered me to go to Huizhao Temple and take the seat of Acharya Xiangxue to lecture on the Direct Explanation of the Brahma Net Sutra, and he asked Master Xiangxue to return to Shita Temple and take the Master's seat to lecture on the Xiaoheng Chao. Both assemblies were completed on the tenth day of the seventh month.

Master Xiang instructed me and my fellow ordinands to go and ask the Master to change the dharma names we had each originally borne, so that we might always attend the Master and serve him. My fellow ordinands did as he said and went to the abbot's quarters, all vying to bow first and ask the Master to grant them dharma names. I alone held back to the last, bowed to the Master, and kneeling on the ground said, 'It was only by my ordaining master's instruction that I was able to rouse the resolve to leave Yunnan and come south to beg the great precepts from the Master. Without my ordaining master I could not have shaved my head and left home, nor could I have received the full precepts and become a true monk. I earnestly beg the Master, in his great compassion, to consent and let me keep my former name, so that I do not forget my root, and I vow to attend the Master's seat all my life.' The Master said, 'After I first received the precepts, my own senior monks urged me to ask the Vinaya Patriarch to change my dharma name. Thinking it over, the Patriarch's name contained the character ru, mine contains ji, and my ordaining master's contains hai; I too did not dare forget my root and change my surname character so as to surpass hai. For over thirty years I have spread the precepts. Today I see that your intention is the same as mine. This is a mind that does not deceive itself! In a good teacher, what matters is conduct and virtue, not what dharma name one bears. I permit you to keep your original name.'

At that time Pini Hermitage in Taixing County invited the Master to open the precepts on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, and everyone went along. On the evening of the tenth day, Precept-Instructing Master Xunliu reported to the Master and asked him to appoint the officers of each hall, saying, 'I am now instructing the new ordinands, but my middle breath is insufficient and my spirit grows weaker by degrees. An Instructing West Hall should be established to direct the precept affairs of every hall, with his seat set in the first hall of the new ordinands. This task can be borne by Jianyue alone. I beg the Master to weigh it with his wisdom and decide.' The Master at once ordered an attendant to gather the community of the two sequences (the monks of a temple, arranged in two ranks east and west below the abbot; the east sequence managed administration, the west sequence managed Dharma affairs) in the abbot's quarters and announced my appointment to them. Kneeling on the ground, I said, 'I only completed the full precepts on the eighth day of the fourth month this year; it is not yet half a year. How would I dare take on such a heavy charge? If I, who am not yet versed in the Vinaya, then teach others, I fear it will harm the new ordinands and betray the Master's compassionate kindness. I beg the Master to choose another among the senior monks who can bear this office and appoint him.' The Master said, 'Xunliu's recommendation is a good one. I too know your mind and your conduct. Even bodhisattvas of the ten grounds still lodge in a position to practise (taking on a post among men in order to aid their practice). For now you may study on your own and teach others at the same time, in appreciation of my intention. Thus one act serves two ends.' The assembly of both sequences said with one voice, 'You should follow the Master's compassionate command and not decline again.' I had no choice but to bow and accept the assignment.

Among my fellow ordinands, Yingzi and Cangwu served as scribes for this precept period, and Huisheng, Yiren, Yuru, Ruoyu, Guanzhi and others served as masters of ceremonies. Everyone strove with all his might, earnest and grave; never before beneath the Master's seat had there been a group so ardent and flourishing as those ordained together at Haichao Hermitage. The Master of Ceremonies of the first hall (who directed all the ceremonial duties) was Eryan, the very Master of Ceremonies under whom I had received the precepts. Though I held a position of authority, in every movement and rest I honored and yielded to him as my teacher. He too did not cling to the notion of self (he was very modest) and in deciding all matters of hall regulation he deferred to me and acted according to my wishes. Yet in my heart I constantly cherished a sense of shame: if someone fond of studying the Vinaya should come to ask me, how could I make him see clearly what was right and wrong, and send him away satisfied? One evening I went to Master Xunliu's cell and told him of my worry. The Master said, 'Among the three baskets of the canon there are more than a thousand fascicles of Mahayana and Hinayana Vinaya, and I have not read them. Since you have this aspiration, you may request them and study as you read. In time you will become a great Vinaya master, and that will be how I do not betray having singled you out in the midst of the great assembly.' So someone was found and sent to Jiaxing, and a copy of the Broad Vinaya was requested and brought back. From then on by day I managed the precept regulations of every hall, and by night I trimmed the lamp and unrolled the scroll, reading and studying in the finest detail. Whenever I met with passages whose words were ancient and whose meaning was hard to grasp, and was at a loss for someone versed in them to consult, I could only close the scroll and sigh. At such times I did nothing but bow and pray to the bodhisattvas, begging them to bless me and open my understanding. Each time, after bowing, I would sit a little while, then unroll the scroll again and ponder its meaning, and it would be like opening a door and seeing the mountain, suddenly clear beyond doubt. Marvelous responses such as this occurred every time.

This precept-transmission assembly was set to conclude on the fifth day of the eleventh month. Three days before the close, the newly ordained disciples of this hall, mindful of my tireless teaching, made together a great yellow silk robe (a monk's robe) to give me, and I said to them, 'The Master and the Precept-Instructing Master entrusted this heavy charge to me, and it is only right that I should exhaust my heart and do my duty and put forth strength to aid the spread of the Dharma. Do you suppose I took the headship in order to seek fame and covet gifts? I gravely declined. They carried the robe to the abbot's quarters, knelt, and explained to the Master the reason for offering it. The Master said to me, 'The Vinaya forbids only covetous seeking; it does not forbid willing donation. You may accept it.' I said, 'There are two reasons why this humble one does not accept the robe. First, I am ashamed that my precept conduct is shallow while my responsibility is heavy, and I fear that where I fall short someone may use it as a ground for slander. Second, the Master's Dharma gate stands high and steep, and I fear that those who hold various offices hereafter may take this as the beginning and set a precedent, and that is why I do not accept it.' The Master approved my thinking and said to the new ordinands, 'The West Hall does not accept this robe because he would preserve his own virtue and protect the Dharma gate. Do not press it on him again!'

On the eighth day of the tenth month I returned with the Master to Shita Temple in Yangzhou. Chengtian Temple in Gaoyou County invited the Master with due ceremony to open the precept transmission on the first day of the twelfth month, to conclude on the fifteenth day of the first month of the new spring, and I again held the office of West Hall.

blocks.text: One Dream, Many Years: Volume Two

inline.s: On the seventeenth day of the first month of the eleventh year of Chongzhen we returned to Shita Temple. At the invitation of Shanqing Hermitage in this prefecture we opened the precepts on the twentieth day of the first month and concluded in the middle of the third month, and I again held the office of First Hall (judging by what precedes, this is probably an error for West Hall). Then at the invitation of Baogong Temple in Shaobo Township we began the period on the eighth day of the fourth month; I held the office of West Hall, and when the precept period ended we returned again to Shita Temple in Yangzhou. In the seventh year of Chongzhen, when the Master was spreading the precepts in Beijing, Princess Rongchang, daughter of Emperor Shenzong, and her consort Lord Yang led all the members of their household to take refuge with the Master and sent envoys to present three golden-tung purple sanghatis (patched outer robes): one to be offered to the Master, one to Acharya Xiangxue, and one to Precept-Instructing Master Xunliu. Now, today, Master Xun brought the robe that the princess and her consort had offered him in those years to the abbot's quarters, bowed, and with tears in his eyes reported to the Master, saying, 'This humble one has attended the Master's seat and held the office of Precept-Instructing Master for eleven years. At all times I have watched and observed the character of each new ordinand and tested his mind and conduct, hoping to find a few men to assist the Master's Dharma gate. Only today, in the precept period at Haichao Hermitage, have I found Jianyue. In my heart I think that of late my appetite has diminished and my spirit has weakened. Before long I shall take leave of this dusty world. I earnestly beg the Master in his compassion to hand on to him this purple robe offered by Princess Rongchang. If I may with my own eyes see that there is someone to succeed me, I shall die content.' The Master gave a long sigh and said, 'You are truly my right-hand disciple, caring for the future of the Dharma gate.' He at once gathered the senior attendants to bear witness, and with his own hand gave me the robe, saying, 'You should serve me as Xunliu has done, and the Dharma gate will flourish!' Tears wet my lapels as I bowed and received it. Of those who gave me birth, my parents; of those who know me, Master Xun. For such great kindness, only benefiting beings can repay it.

In the middle of the sixth month Tandu Temple at Qingjiangpu in Huai'an respectfully invited the Master to open the precepts, and on the nineteenth day of the seventh month the precepts were concluded. The Master wished to go up Mount Yuntai by the Eastern Sea for a joyful visit, and commanded me to stay behind to handle the ordination certificates and the compiling and issuing of the register, and then to dismiss the assembly (let the new ordinands disperse). When that was done, I too went up Mount Yuntai. In the eighth month I went up to report to the Master, and on the thirteenth day I came down the mountain and crossed the sea, returning again to Shita Temple.

Several eminent officials who protected the Dharma in Nanjing invited the Master to open a period at Baoen Temple on the fifteenth day of the tenth month. Master Xunliu lay ill at Shita Temple, and I attended him with broth and medicine and cared for him. This time, when the Master went to the capital to transmit the precepts, Master Duxing served as Acharya and Master Xiangxue as Precept-Instructing Master. Messengers were sent back to call me, but I firmly declined and did not go; afterwards more messengers were sent to call me. Master Xun was by nature extremely dutiful, and said to me, 'Though my illness is grave, you must not disobey the Master's compassionate command. The only thing I have to entrust to you is this: after I am gone, once the cremation (the burning of the body) is done, you may send my relic bones to Tianlong Temple and bury them to the right of the Vinaya Patriarch's stupa.' Hearing this, I could not hold back my tears. I truly did not want to leave him. Master Xun said again, 'This is the Master's first visit to Nanjing; those seeking the precepts will surely be many. Twice he has urgently summoned you, and I think there must be some great matter he wishes to entrust to you. Go quickly, and delay no longer.' I had no choice but to bow and take leave of Master Xun, and went to Nanjing.

The Master asked after Master Xun's illness, and I reported that it was grave. I was again assigned to the office of West Hall. Master Xiangxue also entrusted to me the whole direction of instructing the new ordinands. There were more than six hundred new candidates for the precepts, and the hall where they were lodged stood behind the Hall of the Three Sages of the West. The Master said to me, 'There are many new ordinands, and the two Acharyas who went down before did not arrange the order of their seats. Go down now and arrange it.' I went down at once, and saw luggage scattered in disorder everywhere. Most of those who had come seeking the precepts were men who had studied the sutras and listened to lectures, and not a few had a proud and careless habit, which had to be tamed by a method of self-effacement. So I said to them all, 'By the Master's appointment I come here to bear, however inadequately, the office of West Hall. Now let us consult together. Those willing to obey may dwell in harmony according to the rules; otherwise I cannot look after you all. Please observe this hall: in the middle it is broad, and several hundred people can walk about in it (do walking meditation), while the sleeping platforms around the sides are narrow and cannot hold so many sleepers. If everyone wants to sleep on the high platform (the long communal plank bed), what is to become of the rest? So I intend to assign seats beginning from the floor. Those among you who truly seek the precepts with a sincere heart should yield the good places to others; this will also show the spirit of selflessness and fulfil the bodhisattva's vow. Now let everyone take his place on the floor in order as I direct. The rows must run straight, crosswise and lengthwise, not uneven. Those of you from within the capital, or who have brought your own cot, bring the cot tomorrow and place it according to the seat fixed today. Those from outside the capital, or who have no cot, all go up on the high platform. I hope everyone will keep quiet and not make an uproar!' When they heard this they gladly complied, and there was no scrambling. More than six hundred new ordinands lodged in this great hall, and the rows of seats were so neat and orderly that they looked like streets and lanes; seen at a glance it was truly a magnificent sight.

Every night I expounded the precepts for one double hour, and throughout the day instructed and admonished them as occasion arose, and all of them respected and submitted. When they heard the news that a Master of Witness was to be appointed for the platform (when the platform is formally opened for ordination there must be ten senior and virtuous bhikshus present to bear witness, called the Masters of Witness), the foremost among them, a shramanera (one who has newly left home and received the ten shramanera precepts) named Xiaoyuan, fifty years old, a man of Jingzhou Prefecture, who had long followed the lecture seats in Nanjing, discussed it with his fellow ordinands and wanted to ask me to be the Master of Witness for the platform. Together they went to the abbot's quarters, knelt, and reported their request to the Master. The Master sent an attendant to summon me and explained the matter. I said, 'This humble one's precept years do not amount to two summers (the number of summers that have passed since receiving the full bhikshu precepts), and besides my practice is shallow and I have no virtue of conduct. I dare not place myself in the seat of a Master of Witness.' The Master said, 'This is the united wish of several hundred new ordinands. It is not you setting yourself presumptuously above your place. Do not decline again. This is what is meant by the time and conditions having come!' I had no choice but to bow in thanks, however reluctantly.

The Hall of the Three Sages of the West stood close by the storehouse office (the granary and kitchen), and the gruel and rice of the three periods were taken each on his own seat. One day, when the hour for the morning meal came, the hall servers did not bring the food. I inquired into the reason and learned that the hall servers had demanded money and goods from the new ordinands, and having got none had made trouble for them. I had the hall servers seized at once and punished them with kneeling incense. The hundred or more people in the kitchen then banded together as one faction and all left the Hall of the West. I went to Master Qixuan of the Office of Monastic Registry (the body that managed the register of monks and discipline) and explained the situation. He at once ordered the monks in charge to close every gate of the temple and to lock the storekeeper, the kitchen manager, and the cook in wooden cangues; of the others involved, some climbed the wall and fled. This was an old custom of the kitchen hall in every period of practice in the capital. From this time on it was corrected, and all were diligent and careful to keep the rules, and none dared offend again. On the day when the precepts were formally transmitted and the platform opened, the scene was exactly as I had dreamed that night when I first left home, without the slightest difference.
